tier_reason: Peer-reviewed ESA 2019 paper (LIPIcs vol. 144, 59:1-59:24, doi 10.4230/LIPIcs.ESA.2019.59, cited in the README) whose public benchmark code (benchmark/alias.cpp runs wrs::gsl_alias for construction and queries next to the wrs algorithms; benchmark/bench_intel.sh, bench_all_64.sh, run_seq.sh) compares against the GSL alias table; the GSL figures are known only from search-result summaries because the paper hosts are egress-blocked. Compiler version and CPU models are not in the repo, so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Not on an opened page; search-result summaries of the paper (arXiv 1903.00227 / LIPIcs ESA 2019, both blocked here) report alias-table queries roughly 3-4x faster than GSL 2.5's gsl_ran_discrete (one summary says about 4x at n=10^8, an earlier one more than 3x), attributed to an array-of-structs layout, branchless choice within buckets and a faster random number generator, and Vose-method construction 30% faster than GSL on the Intel machine and 44% faster on the AMD machine. Parallel construction and queries scale near-linearly up to 158 threads.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: C++17, CMake 3.9.2+. CMakeLists.txt adds -march=native, -flto (WRS_USE_LTO on by default), -g, -pthread and warnings; the default build type is Debug unless CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release is passed. Compiler, version and build type used for the paper's runs are not stated in the repo.
corrections.caveats: Snippet only: the paper (arXiv 1903.00227; Dagstuhl LIPIcs ESA 2019; a journal version at dl.acm.org doi 10.1145/3549934 seen only as a search result) is EGRESS_BLOCKED here, so the GSL speedup figures are unverified search-result summaries and differ slightly between results (more than 3x vs about 4x for queries). Part of the query gain comes from a faster random-number generator (optional Intel MKL), not only the table layout. benchmark/alias.cpp notes that, for a fair GSL comparison, the other algorithms must be reconfigured to use size_t indices. The repo README itself states no numbers; CPU models are not named (Intel 80-core/160-thread and AMD 32-core/64-thread machines). Baseline is GSL rather than a C++ standard facility such as std::discrete_distribution. GPL-3.0. Last commit is the dissertation version, 2020-12-09; the ESA version is the esa tag.

notes: Repo, GPL-3.0 license, 21 stars, 2 forks, 8 commits and last commit 2020-12-09 confirmed on github.com; abandoned is correct (>3 years). drops.dagstuhl.de and publikationen.bibliothek.kit.edu were tried once each and are EGRESS_BLOCKED; a paper-based retier to A may be possible if the paper states compiler, flags and CPU models.

tier_reason: First-party README sample output from the repo's own apps/bench_micro.c (xoshiro256 4.00, cromulent128 2.93, splitmix64 1.27, pcg64 1.76 ns/sample over 10^10 samples, seed 69420) with no CPU model, compiler or flags ('a modern CPU', 'exact numbers will vary').

corrections.baseline: xoshiro256++, a 64-bit-state PCG variant labelled pcg64, and splitmix64 (reference copies in src/reference/, timed by the repo's own apps/bench_micro.c)
corrections.caveats: Beats only xoshiro256++ in its own table and loses to the repo's pcg64 and SplitMix64, so it does not clearly beat the named baselines. The repo's 'pcg64' (src/reference/pcg64.c) is not the standard PCG64 (128-bit state, XSL-RR output): it is a 64-bit-state LCG with a pcg32-style XSH-RR permutation. Every generator, including the baselines, is called through a function pointer into a separately compiled static library on global state (no LTO), so call overhead is part of each number; 4.00 ns/sample for xoshiro256++ is slow for that generator. CMakeLists.txt sets no default build type or -O flag, so a plain 'cmake ..' build is unoptimized, and the README does not say which build, compiler or CPU produced the sample output. Young repo (122 commits, all recent) with 0 stars. The AVX2 variant is not benchmarked in the README. Kept as a flagged entry.

notes: Numbers match the README exactly and the 1.37x over xoshiro256++ is correctly marked as derived. MIT license, 0 stars, not a fork, last commit 2026-08-30 confirmed on github.com.

tier_reason: First-party README prose (20x faster than crypto/rand for large data, over 100x in parallel); benchmark code exists in frand_test.go (BenchmarkRead*/BenchmarkReadCrypto*/BenchmarkReadMath* at 1, 4 and 64 goroutines) but no hardware, Go version or results for the current implementation are given.

corrections.caveats: Go package, not callable from C++. The repo does carry benchmark code (frand_test.go: Read at 32 B and 512 KB, sequential, 4 and 64 goroutines, against crypto/rand and math/rand), but the current README gives only ratios with no hardware or Go version. The older README (commit 3f951cc, pre-2024 FKE-CSPRNG implementation) had a table: Read 512kb 5094 MB/s vs crypto/rand 239 MB/s (about 21x, derived from page data) and Read 512kb with 64 goroutines 19665 vs 191 MB/s (about 103x, derived from page data); math/rand was faster for Intn (20 vs 45 ns/op) and Perm(32) (789 vs 954 ns/op); no hardware stated. Since commit 'switch to stdlib ChaCha8 generator' (2024-10-07) frand is a thin wrapper over Go's math/rand/v2 ChaCha8 plus a sync.Pool, so the speedup now belongs mostly to Go's stdlib ChaCha8 over crypto/rand rather than to this package's own code. Not a like-for-like comparison with PCG or xoshiro.

notes: MIT license, 93 stars, 13 forks, 22 commits, last commit 2024-10-07 confirmed on github.com; stale (about two years old) is correct. The record's caveat that there is no benchmark code was wrong and is corrected.
